extracted.intended_audience: Anglo-Saxon scholars, students of English literature, and translators of Old English poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for translating Anglo-Saxon epic verse (Beowulf) into modern English while preserving meter, alliteration, parallelism, and an appropriate archaic flavor, balancing fidelity to the original with readability for modern readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate reproduction of original measures
rubrics_metrics.description: The translator aims to 'reproduce approximately, in modern measures, the venerable epic.' A very close reproduction of Anglo-Saxon verse would, to a large extent, be prose to a modern ear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for an approximation of the original's rhythmic characteristics rather than a literal line-by-line metrical transplant; avoid literalness that results in prose. Emphasize readable cadence appropriate to modern English while retaining essential characteristics of the source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to authoritative text and glossary
rubrics_metrics.description: The Heyne-Socin text and glossary have been closely followed; deviations are made only for good and sufficient reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established critical editions and glossaries as the textual basis; depart from them only with explicit justification or well-argued conjecture. Translator is not primarily an editor, but may occasionally add conjectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance fidelity and readability for dual audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Work is addressed to two classes: Anglo-Saxon scholars (pleased by faithful adherence to the original) and students of English literature (interested in a modern-garb reading).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive to satisfy scholars by preserving key formal and semantic features, while ensuring the translation is engaging and comprehensible to general readers and students; trade-offs between literal fidelity and accessibility should be explicit and defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a regular cadence that permits forward reading
rubrics_metrics.description: To please a larger class of readers, a regular cadence has been used, a measure which, while retaining the essential characteristics of the original, permits the reader to see ahead of him in reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a metrical cadence that creates momentum and anticipatory flow for modern readers; avoid stilted or halting renderings that hinder comprehension or musicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inappropriate modern measures (anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper that grave and solemn speeches be put in ballad measures, or that the rough martial music of Anglo-Saxon verse be interpreted in the smooth measures of modern blank verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not render solemn, archaic, or martial passages into light ballad meters or bland blank verse; choose measures that reflect the tone and force of the original rather than fashionable modern forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain four stresses per half-line with allowance for anacrusis
rubrics_metrics.description: The four stresses of the Anglo-Saxon verse are retained, and as much thesis and anacrusis is allowed as is consistent with a regular cadence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve the four-stress structure characteristic of Old English verse where feasible; permit anacrusis (extra unstressed syllables before the first stress) and thesis to provide natural English phrasing without breaking cadence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use alliteration extensively but not mechanically
rubrics_metrics.description: Alliteration has been used to a large extent; but modern ears would hardly tolerate it on every line. End-rhyme and internal rhyme used occasionally/sporadically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ alliteration as a prominent organizing device, but avoid forcing alliteration into every line; use end-rhyme and internal rhyme sparingly where historically warranted or stylistically effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the 'rime-giver' rule for alliteration
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'rime-giver' has been studiously kept: the first accented syllable in the second half-verse always carries the alliteration; the last accented syllable alliterates only sporadically. Alternate alliteration is occasionally used as in the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When structuring alliterative pairs, ensure the principal alliterative stress occurs on the first accented syllable of the second half-line (the rime-giver); use alternate alliteration where it mirrors the source. Consult original line references for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid adjacent accented syllables except after caesura
rubrics_metrics.description: No two accented syllables have been brought together, except occasionally after a caesural pause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain natural stress patterns by avoiding clustering of strong stresses; allow exceptions only where a caesural pause justifies an unusual stress pairing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrical typology: avoid Sievers's C type; use variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Sievers's C type has been avoided as not consonant with the plan of translation. Several of his types (A, B, variants of D and E) constantly occur; anacrusis gives further variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling Old English meter, prefer a variety of accepted Sievers types (A, B, D, E and variants) and eschew C-type patterns if they conflict with the chosen cadence. Use anacrusis to introduce metrical variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve parallelisms of the original
rubrics_metrics.description: The parallelisms of the original have been faithfully preserved. Occasionally some loss has been sustained; on the other hand, a gain has here and there been made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek to maintain the syntactic and semantic parallel structures characteristic of Old English poetry (repetitions, appositions, kennings). When perfect preservation is impossible, aim for equivalent rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt an appropriate degree of archaism
rubrics_metrics.description: An effort has been made to give a decided flavor of archaism to the translation. All words not in keeping with the spirit of the poem have been avoided. Though many archaic words have been used, there are none believed not to be found in standard modern poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use archaic diction to evoke period flavor, but avoid obscure or invented archaisms that impede comprehension; limit archaism to vocabulary and turns of phrase that are defensible within the norms of modern poetic use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translator's rhetorical model and references
rubrics_metrics.description: The cadences closely resemble those used by Browning in some of his most striking poems; Gummere's 'rime-giver' principle is observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling cadence and rhetorical delivery, consider exemplary modern poets (e.g., Browning) and established metrical theorists; cite and follow recognized principles where they align with the translation's aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural: include translator notes, glossary, and textual apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: The translator closely follows the Heyne-Socin text and glossary and provides a preface, bibliography, glossary of proper names, list of words and phrases not in general use, and textual notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide scholarly apparatus (preface, glossaries, notes, bibliography) to aid readers and scholars; document editorial choices and variant readings to maintain transparency and usefulness for both general and specialist audiences.
